transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-02-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Recording: yes 
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood SE), Dr. Saira Patel (CTO HelioMed), Kenji Mori (Head ML Infra), Laura Gomez (Security), Tom Fischer (PM)

Summary block (auto): SE demo of adaptive hierarchical chunking and eviction heuristics for 128k+ clinical docs. Discussed latency/throughput tradeoffs, quantization choices and private deployment controls. Agreed to POC scope.

00:00 Avery: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're gonna do a deep dive on long context runtime ops. Marco will lead most of the tech bits. quick intro round?
00:18 Saira: hi Saira here, CTO at HelioMed. We ingest long longitudinal patient histories, often >100k tokens for some cohorts. Big constraint: data residency and auditability.
00:30 Kenji: Kenji, I run infra. our current stack is k8s on GCP private VPC, some on prem for regulated workloads. We want to avoid copying data outside our VPC.
00:45 Laura: security, we need KMS integration and full audit trails, plus SAML SSO.
00:55 Avery: great notes — Marco, take it away?
01:03 Marco: yeah thanks. So high level our runtime supports a couple ways to approach 128k+ context. First is chunked append with prefix KV caching. second is hierarchical chunking where you build summarized embeddings at intermediate layers. third is sharded attention where we split long sequences across devices. I'm gonna sketch trade-offs.
01:30 Kenji: quick q — what's the perf hit when you do hierarchical vs naive append?
01:37 Marco: good q. naive append with continuous KV will see linear memory growth and latency depending on sequence length. with hierarchical chunking you pay extra compute to compress chunks, but KV working set drops and tail latency improves for retrieval heavy patterns. for our benchmark on a 128k doc with a 4k live window we saw p95 reduce by roughly 30% in the simulated run. caveat: numbers vary by prompt pattern.
02:05 Saira: when you say compress chunks, is that lossy? clinical accuracy is critical — we can't drop details that affect decisions.
02:15 Marco: yep — it's lossy unless you keep the original KV on cold storage. Our approach is multi-tier: hot KV kept in fast GPU-resident memory for recent tokens; mid-tier uses compressed summaries (chunk embeddings + key pointers), and cold tier persists full segments in object storage with deterministic retrieval. So you can always rehydrate if exact detail is needed, but that adds IO latency.
02:40 Tom: that's interesting. So a retrieval path would first hit hot KV, then fallback to mid-tier reify?
02:47 Marco: exactly. We also do adaptive eviction: hotness is tracked by token access frequency and recency; tokens above threshold remain resident. The eviction uses a weighted LRU + token importance heuristic (derived from query embeddings).
03:05 Laura: sounds complex — does that create extra audit surfaces? We need to log which tier served the response.
03:12 Marco: yes, Redwood Console exposes per-request traces showing tier hits, KV hit/miss, and latency breakdown. We can push those logs to your SIEM via syslog or Cloud Pub/Sub.
03:22 Laura: good. also: KMS—where are keys stored for Private deployments?
03:26 Avery: for Private (VPC) we support customer-managed KMS or HSM. Keys never leave your control plane; Redwood can integrate with Cloud KMS, AWS KMS, or an on-prem HSM via PKCS11.
03:38 Kenji: good. network wise we'll want egress locked and no internet-facing endpoints. is Redwood Private fully air-gapped option?
03:45 Marco: we have an on-prem packaged deploy that can be deployed behind a firewall. There are some managed control-plane features that require connectivity for updates but we have an offline bootstrap path. We'll share the install checklist.
03:58 Avery: let's pivot back to latency/throughput: Marco, can you walk numbers for batching and quantization choices?
04:05 Marco: sure. For very long contexts, batching helps throughput but increases tail latency. We recommend dynamic batching with a tight latency SLO: small batches for latency-critical queries (e.g., interactive assistant) and larger for async bulk processing (e.g., batch summarization). For quantization: Q4_0 and Q5_0 give large memory wins, but some models with sensitive clinical terminology showed small accuracy regressions; Q8 or bf16 keeps quality but costs more. We suggested running evals against your prompt set.
04:40 Saira: can we see delta in hallucination or clinical precision with 4-bit quant?
04:45 Marco: in our evals on similar corpora, F1 for entity extraction dropped 1-3% with aggressive 4-bit configs. Also corner cases with rare biomarkers were affected. So for HelioMed we recommend hybrid: keep core NER and hallucination-sensitive layers in higher precision, quantize the rest. Redwood runtime supports mixed-precision on-the-fly.
05:10 Kenji: do you have tooling to automate which layers to keep high precision?
05:15 Marco: yes we have a recommendation engine in Redwood Optimize that suggests per-layer quant profiles based on your evals. we'll share a sample report.
05:25 Tom: about KV eviction — how do you ensure cold rehydrate doesn't blow up tail latency for a live flow?
05:31 Marco: fallback policies: we can do async rehydrate where initial response uses mid-tier summary and trigger background rehydration to update cache for subsequent queries. For synchronous exact answers we surface a progressive response: first give summarized answer (low latency) then stream a rehydrated append if user requests details.
05:55 Saira: hmm we need strict SLOs on patient-facing features. If a clinician requests full history, we can't return partial without highlighting. UI/UX side is fine but we need deterministic billing and latency for those exact calls.
06:08 Avery: noted — we'll include cost models for sync rehydrate vs async in the POC proposal.
06:15 Marco: quick demo: I have a simulated run here — running a 128k doc split into 4k chunks with 512-token overlap, hierarchical summaries every 16 chunks. (screen share) p50 is ~220ms for local window ops, p95 ~1.1s when doing mid-tier rehydrates, p99 spikes to 3.8s when cold fetch hits object store. These were on 8 V100-equivalent GPUs with pinned KV memory.
07:00 Kenji: what's the cost differential if we go to A100s or H100s?
07:06 Marco: H100s reduce end-to-end latency by ~20-30% for attention-heavy ops, and allow larger resident KV due to higher HBM; but unit cost is higher. We can model per-token cost for both.
07:18 Laura: are there any known issues with sparse attention or rotary embedding interaction when quantizing?
07:24 Marco: good catch. Sparse attention kernels and rotary embeddings are generally fine, but quantization on the rotary coefficients can introduce small numeric drift — we've added corrective scaling in the runtime to mitigate that. We'll include a note in the tech brief.
07:40 Saira: on data flows — will any data be cached outside our VPC for Redwood Dedicated?
07:46 Avery: Dedicated can be provisioned inside your VPC with private networking; we can guarantee that tokenization and KV stays within your network if you choose private deployment. For hosted Redwood API, we'd need to discuss residency.
08:00 Kenji: sync question — does Redwood persist logs or transcripts with PII? We need to scrub PHI and retain only audit pointers.
08:09 Marco: by default we don't keep user payloads for hosted, and for Private you control persistence. We also support token redaction and a policy layer to strip or hash PHI before caching. We can show config examples.
08:25 Tom: how do you validate chunk boundaries so we don't break clinical sentences? losing context split in the middle of an Rx could be problematic.
08:33 Marco: we use semantic-aware chunking: boundary detection via sentence/section heuristics plus an overlap window. We bias chunk boundaries at section headers (e.g., 'Medication History') and keep semantic units intact with overlap to ensure cross-boundary references are preserved.
08:55 Saira: performance on multi-query threads — clinicians will jump around different parts of the record, not just append. How does hot tier handle random access?
09:04 Marco: hot tier assigns token scores based on query access patterns; few-shot queries to disparate regions trigger fetch and temporarily warm those segments. We also support pre-warming based on predicted next-query heuristics (e.g., follow-up queries when a clinician drills into labs).
09:25 Kenji: what's the expected network IO if warm segments are rehydrated from object storage frequently?
09:30 Marco: depends on size; for typical 4k chunk objects, rehydration is ~70-120ms if storage is in same region and using high IOPS. Cold fetch across regions will be much worse. That's why placement matters.
09:50 Laura: security again — can we get a diagram of the network flow and where logs are stored?
09:55 Avery: yes, we'll attach a network diagram and the private deployment checklist in the follow-up.
10:03 Marco: quick note about batching: we support prefix-aware batching where requests that share early tokens get coalesced but requests with different prefixes avoid being batched together to prevent incorrect cache reuse. That helps optimize both throughput and correctness.
10:25 Saira: okay timeboxing — what are the realistic POC acceptance criteria?
10:30 Avery: proposed acceptance criteria: 1) p95 interactive query latency < 1.5s for queries hitting hot tier, 2) end-to-end correctness on 200 validation prompts (entity extraction precision > 95%), 3) no PII exfiltration, logs and auditability validated, 4) deployment in Private VPC with customer-managed KMS.
10:52 Tom: I'd add viability target: cost per full-document summary under $X (we'll define offline).
10:58 Avery: sure we'll model that.
11:05 Marco: last bits — quantization profile recommendation: Hybrid (keep embedding and decoder head in fp16/bf16, quantize transformer blocks to Q4_0 except last 2 blocks). We'll run on your prompts and send delta metrics.
11:20 Kenji: and rolling KV eviction thresholds? we want to set policies per team.
11:26 Marco: policy knob example: keep hotness threshold adjustable (%, absolute memory cap), TTL for mid-tier, and priority labels to pin segments (e.g., regulatory documents). We'll include UI screenshots of Redwood Console.
11:40 Saira: great. can you also include the legal checklist for on-prem?
11:44 Avery: yes, it's in the enterprise pack. we'll attach SOC2, ISO, encryption and IP terms.
11:51 Marco: wrapping up — we'll run the microbench and send a lab notebook with p50/p95/p99 and KV stats.
11:58 Avery: recap of next steps... (recap) send POC proposal, microbench, sample config, security docs, and schedule kickoff. Thanks everyone.
12:10 Saira: thanks, we look forward to the POC.
